title: Using Claude and ChatGPT to knock out a bunch of prototypes of my game ideas is amazing
author: 74BIT
selftext:
So yeah, the tools are getting better and I couldnt be happier.

I have an ambition to create around 10 small game prototypes in HTML using Claude or ChatGPT. See which ones take off and build one for Steam Next Fest this October.

This is my latest. A foray into 3d platforming. 

Its still rough (bugs for sure) but I was able to visualize the core loop, 3 planets (and tutorial planetoid), mechanics, procedural systems and establish a workflow with ChatGPT and Blockbench.

Become Yorick the Life Reaper. Travel to worlds that are lifeless, reap dead matter and bloom the worlds back to life! You can reshape the world with these abilities. Speaking of which, there is a Skill Tree you can upgrade Yorick's abilities. And yes, it is Yorick from Hamlet. It is a bit of my take on how life and death are a cycle. The undiscovered country!!!

If your curious check it out here. Its free and plays in browser.  
Let me know what you think!

[https://itch.io/dashboard](https://itch.io/dashboard)

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body:
Its hard to say. 

Fable was pretty great like a week ago.

I just built 2 small html prototypes of the same game in Claude Fable and ChatGPT Sol yesterday using a design doc prompt for both. 

Fable missed some of the core mechanics, controls were a bit messed up.

Sol got most of it right and the visuals, presentation (including start screen), controls were better. 

They both didnt make the game look great and it still needed a lot of work.

Right now I feel like Sol is pretty good and follows directions better.

comments.author: Capitinefrobou
comments.body: I wonder if you could gimme some tips over your workflow prototyping these games, etc? I'd love to do the same but still figuring out a good workflow!

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body:
This is how I basically worked with this project

**Come up with core Idea → research similar games → simplify the core loop → establish art direction (keep low) → build a rough HTML prototype → test constantly → add worlds and systems → replace generic content with authored content (using Blockbench since it is voxels) → polish presentation → fix mobile and persistence → audit everything → release a testable build.**

I acted **like a creative director and hands-on tester**: I defined what the experience should feel like, using AI to create and implement it, test the result yourself, and then give highly specific visual, mechanical, and technical corrections.

Also keep in mind, I had the prototype mentality. Make it exist first then worry about bugs or flaws later. Do not get trapped in perfection. If it is a prototype, I focused on getting the core idea, game feel, mood, character movement feel, etc. Not how perfectly this one detail looks. I have an art background and my struggle is letting go of a visual and not wasting too much time making it pretty.

Hope this helps.

If you have more questions feel free to ask!

replies.author: bonsoir-world
replies.body:
This is only html? 

Did you plug into any other tools with Claude/ChatGPT? 

For steam what is your plans? To develop fully? Any ideas on tooling or MCP integrations? 

I have so many ideas but i’m not at all a game dev. I’m hoping to make some prototypes I can use to either build a team for, crowdfund or get investment on! 

This is really cool!

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body:
Yes. I am prototyping in HTML first to go fast and knock out the prototype.   
  
I only used Blockbench to modify/build some of the ingame models (Spirit Animals and main character). 

For Steam, I will probably use the current prototype, take in user input, rebuild it in Unity or Godot with AI (havent picked one just yet, depends on the usabilty) doing the coding. Possibly have it also create 3d models visuals for me.

Its funny because when I was making my first few games, coding and tech barriers consumed my brainspace and really bogged me down. But now, with the advent of these AI tools, my brain is open to thinking about the new ideas I want to do and not "hmm not sure how I can do that". Its unlocked my creativity.

That is another thing I dont have experience with. Crowdfunding or investment. I need to learn more.

Yeah it is amazing. Its fun and addicting to make your own thing with you in the driver seat.

comments.author: ellipticbadger
comments.body: Could you tell us what if any libs / tools Claude chose for the prototype?

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body:
**Runtime (shipped in the game)**

**Libraries**

	**•**	Three.js r128 (cdnjs) — the only external dependency

**Browser APIs**

	**•**	WebGL (via Three.js)  
	**•**	WebAudio API  
	**•**	Canvas 2D  
	**•**	localStorage  
	**•**	Pointer Lock API  
	**•**	Touch Events  
	**•**	requestAnimationFrame  
	**•**	CSS animations  
	**•**	Inline SVG

**Assets**

	**•**	Post-processing pipeline  
	**•**	Noise functions  
	**•**	Seeded RNG  
	**•**	Blockbench model loader  
	**•**	Movement/collision  
	**•**	Camera controls  
	**•**	Music and SFX synthesis  
	**•**	UI framework

**Dev tools**

	**•**	Blockbench (Bedrock Model format)  
	**•**	Python (rep() patch scripts)  
	**•**	Node.js (node --check, headless test suites)  
	**•**	Three.js r128 via npm (headless sims)  
	**•**	@shaderfrog/glsl-parser  
	**•**	Git  
	**•**	25-suite test harness

comments.author: YairHairNow
comments.body:
Don't believe the 1shot GTA/AAA prompts. It's terrible clickbait spam.   
  
This is like a 5 shot prompt in reality. I don't doubt we'll be 1-shotting AAA games 1-2 years from now. But we're barely skimming the surface for 3D fr. 

You need a fuckton of assets and the 3D understanding is just now getting honed in with models.

comments.author: MintL1
comments.body:
How much adjustments do you need to make something as visually pleasing? I guess this is not a one prompt prototype.

I wonder if I should make bigger few prompts or many small prompts specifically to small details?

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body:
It took a bit of tweaking. Definitely not one big prompt.

Part of it is seeing it in the game and judging if it looks good or is the right technique

I would create a small vision of what you want it to look like. Maybe show a visual, have it break it down of what makes the image look the way it does then start prompting parts at a time.

It doesnt get it right or it can be very literal sometimes.

comments.author: Beatsu
comments.body: How long did it take for you to build this? And how do you prompt to get something like this?

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body: I worked it in my free time for about 2.5 weeks. Prompting…well that is a longer story. You need a clear vision for your idea first. Then create a plan, how you want the game to look. Then start building part by part. This was not a one big shot prompt. It took many with direction and testing from me. You can see more info on my process if you scroll down a bit in the conversation with Capitinefrobou.

replies.author: 74BIT
replies.body: I used to work at EA many years ago but I was on the Art side. For the past 5 or so years, I have been making small games as a hobby. I have some base knowledge but I am not a programmer. From what I have heard online, Godot works well with AI. I havent tried using it with Unity, Godot or Unreal yet. This game is in HTML for the purpose of prototyping. Speed and proof of concept. My recommendation is to find out your core game loop, find if it is fun as soon as you can. Dont let anything get in the way of that at first. This is why I use HTML Threejs (prompting with Claude or ChatGPT. Feel free to message me directly for more questions.
